notes.body_html: Asarah Maamaros (Maamar Chikur Din I:14): “The Sages already noted, saying that on account of a single individual who did teshuvah such as this, they forgive the entire community. The explanation [of the Rav] is: their portion in the oath [at Sinai] — being sureties one for another — is what is pardoned in his merit; and this is correct.” The commentary Yad Yehudah explains: the Rav means that the community’s being forgiven through the individual’s teshuvah refers to that very sin of that individual — and they forgive the community their guarantorship [liability], since all Israel are guarantors one for another, as the Sages expounded on “and they shall stumble one over another” (Vayikra 26:37) — [each] over his brother’s sin. R’ Tzadok rejects this reading in favor of the plain sense: the penitent’s forgiveness truly extends to the whole world.

notes.body_html: Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados, Yoma 86b (on “on account of an individual [who repents] they forgive the whole world”): He proposes to explain it as the Gemara says at the end of the first chapter of Kiddushin (40b) — a person should always regard the world as half innocent and half guilty; if he performs one mitzvah, fortunate is he, for he has tipped the whole world to the scale of merit. So here: even if the world is mostly guilty, if this one does complete teshuvah out of love, his willful sins become merits, and he thereby tips the entire world to the scale of merit, so that the whole world is forgiven. R’ Tzadok finds this forced, preferring that the individual penitent’s teshuvah itself — as the “heart” of the collective stature — draws healing to all.

notes.body_html: “There is nothing that stands before teshuvah” (Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 3:14): having enumerated those who forfeit their share in the World to Come, the Rambam rules that even they — “if he repented from his wickedness and died as a baal teshuvah, he is among the people of the World to Come; for there is nothing that stands before teshuvah [she-ein lecha davar she-omed bifnei ha-teshuvah] — even one who denied the Ikkar all his days and repented at the last has a share in the World to Come.” Meforshim: the Rambam anchors this in “Peace, peace, to the far and to the near, says Hashem — and I will heal him” (Yeshayah 57:19) — the “far one” being the lifelong sinner whom teshuvah heals and draws near; it is the boundlessness of teshuvah’s reach, halted by no prior sin. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is precisely “the last and seventh rung in the greatness of teshuvah” — teshuvah “in the ultimate perfection of its expansion, which is ‘without bounds’ [b’lo meitzarim — evoking the limitless nachalah b’li metzarim of Shabbos 118a]” — so potent that when a single individual truly repents, “they forgive him and the whole world with him.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּשְׁמוֹת רַבָּה] עַל פָּסוּק ״אֵיפֹה הָיִיתָ בְּיָסְדִי אָרֶץ״
notes.body_html: Iyov 38:4 (Midrash): on “Where were you when I founded the earth?”, the Midrash teaches that the souls of all Israel were present, included within Adam HaRishon, at the founding of the world — the basis for R’ Tzadok’s point that all souls form a single “stature” and are bound up with one another from the very beginning of Creation.Chabad context - Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, ch. 32: The Alter Rebbe gives a particularly clear Chassidic formulation of the ontological unity that R' Tzadok uses here. All Israel, he writes, are literally brothers because 'kulan mat'imos ve'Av echad lekulanah' - all their souls correspond and share one Father - and therefore 'all Israel are called actual brothers from the root of their souls in Hashem Echad; only the bodies are divided.' The division belongs to bodily embodiment; at the level of shoresh haneshamah the many are already one. He therefore explains that the indwelling of the Divine light in Knesses Yisrael requires the souls to be joined 'lemehevei echad be'echad,' because the Shechinah does not rest in a place of spiritual fracture. This supplies an exact Chassidic background to R' Tzadok's insistence that the souls are not merely a federation of individuals who happen to share responsibility, but one complete komah. If the bodies are the principle, each person appears self-contained; if the soul-root is the principle, another Jew's deficiency is a deficiency in the same living unity. The extraordinary statement that one individual's complete teshuvah can extend forgiveness beyond himself thus begins from a metaphysical premise rather than a legal fiction: the individual who returns is not an isolated point. His movement occurs within the shared root in which Knesses Yisrael is already 'one in One.'

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְגַם חָכְמָתוֹ שֶׁבְּמוֹחוֹ וּבִינָתוֹ שֶׁבְּלִבּוֹ, אֵבָרִים הָרָאשִׁים שֶׁבּוֹ, אֵין מְיוּשָּׁבִים עַל יְדֵי זֶה הַכְּאֵב שֶׁבִּקְצֵה אֵבֶר הַיּוֹתֵר קָטָן
notes.body_html: Cf. Shevuos 39a (and Sanhedrin 27b): “all Israel are guarantors one for another [arevim zeh ba-zeh]” — the halachic root of the mutual bond underlying this siman. Maharal reads this principle through the very image R’ Tzadok uses here: Israel “are like a single man, so that if there is a wound in one of his limbs, all the limbs feel it, since they are one body.”Chassidic parallel - Be'er Mayim Chaim, Emor 21:1:2: The Be'er Mayim Chaim states almost the same bodily model as this se'if and pushes it to the same conclusion. 'Kol Yisrael guf echad heim' - all Israel are one body. Some souls function as the head, the 'rashei alfei Yisrael'; some as the eyes; the masses correspond to the lower limbs, legs and heels, but all together form one body of 248 limbs and 365 sinews. From this he draws a striking consequence: so long as the whole of Israel has not reached shleimus, even the choicest souls and the heads of Israel are not themselves complete, because blessing rests only upon a complete thing. He cites Chazal that Shmuel was worthy of a level of Shechinah comparable to Moshe but his generation was not worthy, and reads this literally through the common body: the imperfection of the generation limited the head. Conversely, the good of Israel raises its leaders. The same passage explains arvus from this bodily unity and compares harming another Jew to a hand striking another limb of one's own body. This is an unusually exact complement to R' Tzadok's claim that one unrectified spark leaves a chisaron in the entire komah. The common body means that completion cannot be purely private. It also explains why the ultimate teshuvah of the 'heart' or head can reverberate through the whole organism: the channels of merit and deficiency already run through a single living body before the individual act of return takes place.

notes.body_html: Mishlei 4:23: “מִכׇּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ, כִּי מִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים” — “above all that you guard, guard your heart, for from it are the issues of life.” Meforshim: Rashi — guard your heart, more than any other watch, from evil thoughts; “for from it are the issues of life,” since the vitality of the whole body depends upon the heart. Metzudas David — the heart is the wellspring of life to all the limbs, and therefore must be guarded above all. R’ Tzadok’s use: the heart is “the wellsprings of life to the whole body,” so that “when the heart is in wholeness there is no spoilage in any limb,” and every healing flows from the heart, which “draws new blood and new vitality” to the ailing limb; and in each generation there is one soul who is “the heart of that generation,” the source of its life and the awakener of its teshuvah — and David, who “raised up the yoke of teshuvah,” is “the heart of the whole of Israel,” and therefore merited kingship.

notes.body_html: Sefer Yetzirah likens the ordering of the body to the ordering of the cosmos — “the heart in the body is like a king in the world” — the heart ruling and vivifying the limbs as a king rules his realm. Hence David, the “heart” of Israel and the awakener of its teshuvah, is fittingly the bearer of kingship.Direct Chabad parallel - Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, ch. 2: Tanya gives the organic hierarchy that stands immediately behind R' Tzadok's image of one soul as the 'heart' of a generation. Although there are innumerable levels of Jewish souls, the Alter Rebbe says, in every generation there are 'rashei alfei Yisrael' whose souls are literally the aspect of head and brain in relation to the souls of the populace. He then extends the bodily analogy down to the lowest level: even the toenails of a son still derive their vitality from the brain in the head, and likewise the vitality of the souls of ordinary Jews is drawn through the souls of the tzaddikim and sages who are the 'heads of the children of Israel' in their generation. This does not erase the individuality of the limbs; it explains how differentiated members remain one organism and how life can pass from a governing organ to the whole body. R' Tzadok identifies the decisive organ here not simply as the brain but as the heart, because 'mimenu totze'os chayim' and because teshuvah is principally an awakening of the heart. The two formulations therefore complement one another: Tanya provides the Chassidic anatomy of generational interdependence, while R' Tzadok identifies Davidic teshuvah as the pulse by which renewed life enters that organism. When the generational 'heart' returns in completeness, it is not merely setting a public example; it is renewing the flow of chiyus within the body to which all the other souls belong.

notes.body_html: “One who breathes, breathes from within himself” (the Kabbalistic principle; cf. Ramban, Bereishis 2:7): explaining why the neshamah is “a portion of God from above” (Iyov 31:2), the tradition holds “man de-nafach mi-tocheih nafach” — one who blows breathes out from his own inner self; so when “He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Bereishis 2:7), the soul given was from His very essence. Meforshim: the Ramban (Bereishis 2:7) — “he who breathes into the nostrils of another gives into him something of his own soul… the soul in man is of Divine essence,” from the foundation of Binah, “for the breath of Shaddai gives them understanding” (Iyov 32:8). R’ Tzadok’s use: the souls of Knesses Yisrael are literally “a portion of God from above,” emanated from His holy essence “when it arose in His will to be a place for the creation of worlds” — the lowest of the emanated rungs, yet the one able to clothe the Shechinah in this physical world.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Miketz §14): "“between light and darkness” — this is the holiness of the month, through the illumination of the moon; “and between Israel and the peoples” — this is the holiness of the circumcision, which separates between Israel and the peoples; “and between the seventh day and the six days of work” —" Exactly the se’if: the whole purpose of Creation is a dwelling below, and the marks of that dwelling are the very separations by which the lower world is bounded and made fit to hold it.Chabad context - Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, ch. 36: The Alter Rebbe formulates the purpose of Creation in terms that are nearly identical to R' Tzadok's description of Malchus as the final rung for whose sake the whole descent exists: 'tachlis bri'as olam hazeh hu shenis'aveh HaKadosh Baruch Hu lihyos lo dirah batachtonim.' The purpose of the entire hishtalshelus, he stresses, is not the higher worlds, for from their perspective every descent is a diminution of revealed light; the purpose is specifically this lowest physical world, the place of the greatest concealment, so that darkness itself may be transformed and the Infinite light revealed precisely there. He then says that the days of Mashiach, and especially techiyas hameisim, are the tachlis and shleimus of the creation of this world 'shelechach nivra mitchilaso' - the consummation for which it was created from the beginning. This provides a powerful parallel to R' Tzadok's 'achor va-kedem' structure. The tachton is chronologically and spiritually last, yet in intention it is first; the lowest point is the destination toward which the entire chain of worlds was ordered. Malchus is therefore precious not in spite of being the final receptacle but precisely because only there does the original Divine desire reach actuality. Teshuvah's seventh rung belongs to Malchus for the same reason: the final rectification is not an escape from the lower world but the disclosure that the lower world and the collective human stature were the intended dwelling from the outset.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 139:5: “אָחוֹר וָקֶדֶם צַרְתָּנִי, וַתָּשֶׁת עָלַי כַּפֶּכָה” — “back and front You have formed me, and laid Your hand upon me.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak read it of God’s all-encompassing formation of man — fashioning him “behind and before,” enclosing him on every side. Chazal (Berachos 61a; Eruvin 18a) expound “achor va-kedem” of Adam HaRishon, created “du-partzufin” — with two faces, back and front. R’ Tzadok’s use: he reads it of man’s place in the order of creation — man is “achor,” the last of all creatures (“the end of the deed”), yet also “kedem,” the first and head (“thought first”), “for on this was the first intent in the creation of the world”; when he reaches his perfection, and the whole purpose of Creation is fulfilled through him, he is revealed as its very head.

This makes precise why R' Tzadok does not treat the ascent of the final heh as an accidental promotion of what was originally low. The end becomes a crown because the beginning was hidden in the end all along. The lower land is the arena where the intention that preceded the chain of emanation becomes an accomplished reality, and therefore its completed form can rise above the stages that merely transmitted the intention. In this light, 'ateres ba'alah' is not an inversion of the created order but its disclosure: what appeared as recipient is shown to have carried the deepest ratzon from the first. This also clarifies the relation between teshuvah and the seventh middah. notes.body_html: Mishnah, Sanhedrin 90a (Perek Chelek): “All Israel have a share in the World to Come, as it says, ‘and your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever’ (Yeshayah 60:21).” R’ Tzadok reads “land [eretz]” as the lowest rung (Malchus) which, in the Future, is itself transformed into “the upper land” — so that inheriting the land is the inheritance of Olam Haba.Izhbitz-Radzin context - Sod Yesharim, Yom Kippur 6:1: R. Gershon Henoch of Radzin develops Malchus in a way that strikingly complements the present se'if. Malchus is the final middah, he writes, 'shebah nigmar hahavayah mikol seder hahishtalshelus bishleimus hagamur'; it is the last point of concealment, so distant from the source that Creation can appear to possess an independent existence. Precisely that concealment makes bechirah and coronation possible: the creature can stand within apparent independence and nevertheless choose to crown Hashem. Malchus is therefore 'leis lah migarmah klum' and yet the completion of all the middos, because its entire action is an or chozer that recognizes and returns the upper will. Sod Yesharim then explains the moon's claim of two kings using one crown: since the whole Divine intention reaches completion through Malchus, she senses a genuine root-superiority. In the present world, however, evil is not yet fully clarified, so Malchus must accept tzimtzum - 'lechi u'ma'ati es atzmech.' Only in the Future, after the birurim are complete, will 'eishes chayil ateres ba'alah' be openly true and 'Keser Elyon ihu Keser Malchus' become revealed. This distinction is exactly the one R' Tzadok needs. The final heh is rooted above the six middos, but its superiority cannot yet be lived as unrestricted self-assertion. Present avodah requires constriction, humility and Torah-defined bechirah; future shleimus reveals why the lowest, after faithfully completing its task, was rooted in the highest all along.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §51): “It is known that Adam is the acronym of Adam–David–Mashiach, for all is one — since the world is like a sphere (as it says in the Yerushalmi, Avodah Zarah), and in a sphere the beginning and the end are one point; so too Adam and Mashiach, that is, David — all is one.” The “end of the deed” (David) and the “thought that was first” meet: Adam, David, and Mashiach are one root-soul, the beginning embedded in the end.Early Chassidic parallel - Me'or Einayim, Pinchas 13: The Me'or Einayim gives an exceptionally close Chassidic account of the Adam-David-Mashiach structure used here. Citing the teaching of the Baal Shem Tov, he writes that every Jew must 'repair and prepare the portion of the stature of Mashiach that belongs to his soul.' Adam is read as the roshei teivos Adam-David-Mashiach. Adam HaRishon's original stature extended from one end of the world to the other because all the souls of Israel were included within him; after the sin that stature was diminished. Mashiach will once again be 'komah sheleimah mikol nishmos Yisrael,' a complete stature composed of the entirety of Jewish souls, corresponding to Adam before the sin. Consequently, the building of Mashiach is not external to the avodah of ordinary souls: each person must prepare his own chelek until the entire stature is repaired and a permanent universal yichud becomes possible. This sheds unusually direct light on R' Tzadok's statement that Mashiach is David himself at the level of root, while David is the beginning of the effort from 'sof ma'aseh' and Mashiach is its completed form as it stands in 'machshavah techilah.' The continuity is not merely genealogical. Adam, David and Mashiach are names for successive states of one collective human-Jewish komah: primordial inclusion, historical repair through teshuvah, and final reintegration. Me'or Einayim also prevents the doctrine from becoming passive: because every soul constitutes a limb of that future stature, each individual's present avodah literally belongs to the construction of the completed Mashiach.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §18): “As Korach’s assembly claimed, that ‘the whole congregation are all holy’ and worthy of the high priesthood — and Moshe Rabbeinu showed them that it is not so in actuality in this world, [where] the revelation of their holiness [is not yet manifest]; and only ‘the one whom Hashem chooses’ is holy in actuality among the souls. So too with the days [of the year]; and the World to Come is called (end of Tamid) ‘a day that is wholly Shabbos,’ for [then] there is no division of times, since all is holy.” Korach’s claim was true at the root — the Shechinah did rest in all — but its full manifestation awaits the Future, when the whole nation stands “like David.”Direct Izhbitz source - Mei HaShiloach I, Korach 3: R. Mordechai Yosef addresses Korach's exact claim and makes the temporal distinction that R' Tzadok develops here. Korach argued that there should be no superiority of one Jew over another because 'betocham Hashem' - Hashem dwells within all of them equally. Mei HaShiloach says that this describes the Future, when Hashem will make a machol, a circle, for the tzaddikim: in a circle there is no point intrinsically closer to the center than another. Korach's error was to insist 'she'atah gam kein hu kach' - that the future equality was already the operative order of the present. The Izhbitzer then turns Korach's own history against him: when the crown and distinction of Levi were given to him, he did not protest that Israel admits no hierarchy. This is an extraordinarily precise complement to R' Tzadok's reading. 'Kulam kedoshim' is not dismissed as false; it is a truth of shoresh and destiny. Yet the world of avodah before final birur still contains differentiated offices, chosen vessels and unequal degrees of revealed kedushah. To collapse the future root into the present state is itself a distortion of that root. R' Tzadok can therefore say both that the claim was true enough to be written in Torah and that Moshe's distinction remained necessary. The completed seventh rung of teshuvah is what finally allows the circular truth to become manifest without destroying the ordered avodah through which that completion is reached.

notes.body_html: Gittin 62a: When Geneiva passed Rav Huna and Rav Chisda, he greeted them, “Peace upon you, kings!” They asked, “From where [do you know] that the Rabbis are called kings?” He answered, “As it is written, ‘By me kings reign’ (Mishlei 8:15)” — i.e., through the Torah. Hence “who are kings? — the Rabbis”: the wilderness generation would have needed no king but the Torah-authority of its Sages.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah §23): “and so in the Future the two Mashiachs will come — Mashiach ben Yosef, who will clarify all Israel” Exactly the se’if: the seventh rung that “forgives the whole world entire” is a work of clarification performed upon all Israel together, not a pardon granted to each separately.Izhbitz-Radzin culmination - Tiferet Yosef, Hoshana Rabba 4: Tiferet Yosef describes David's distinctive middah in language that almost states the conclusion of this siman. David refuses to take personal spiritual force even from his own mesirus nefesh; he returns the power of avodah itself to Hashem and recognizes that 'all his strength and all the strength of his service is entirely from Hashem.' From that radical bittul, R. Yosef explains, a new capacity emerges: one who does not appropriate even his own righteousness can 'give a place to the whole creation' and can find a defense even for those whose deeds appeared until now to be without light. notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Lag BaOmer §8): “the conclusion of Shas, with the teaching of Tanna d’Bei Eliyahu, "whoever studies… is assured that he is a son of the World to Come"; and we have said that the meaning of "assured that he is a son of the World to Come," and not "designated for the World to Come," is that he merits to taste in his lifetime a foretaste of the World to Come — that in his very lifetime he is a son of the World to Come.” Exactly the se’if’s seventh elevation: the final rung is not only awaited but tasted here, which is why it can be borne by an individual of David’s seed within this world.Chassidic synthesis - Tiferet Shlomo, Shabbat HaGadol 4: The Tiferet Shlomo identifies Mashiach with the completion of the very stature that R' Tzadok has traced from Adam through David. He notes the familiar remez Adam-David-Mashiach and calls Mashiach 'gemar hatikkun bechol komas Adam HaRishon' - the completion of the rectification of the entire stature of Adam HaRishon. The significance of this formulation is that the final redemption is not simply the arrival of an extraordinary righteous person alongside an otherwise unchanged humanity. The stature itself is what reaches tikkun. That language helps gather the preceding se'ifim of this siman into one point: all souls were included in Adam; David becomes the heart of teshuvah within the fractured historical body; Mashiach is the completed Adamic stature in which the dispersed limbs have reached their intended relation and the original life can flow without the obstruction of sin and death. It also explains why the seventh greatness of teshuvah necessarily has a universal horizon. If Mashiach were only a private tzaddik, his perfection would remain one local excellence among many. If he is the 'gemar hatikkun' of Adam's whole komah, then his Davidic teshuvah belongs by definition to the structure in which the lives of all Israel are included. R' Tzadok's conclusion - the disappearance of the yetzer and death and the inability to find Israel's sin - is therefore not an additional miracle after teshuvah; it is what the complete repair of the collective Adam means when the final limb of the historical stature has returned to its root.
